content.intro: In this lesson, you will explore creating your first xml file within XML Environment Setup and First Document. You will connect its syllabus topics to an inspectable example, check the expected result, and note tool/version limits.
content.why_it_matters: Creating Your First XML File matters because XML workflows rely on explicit structure and predictable processing. The lesson helps you reason about creating a .xml file, avoid a common misunderstanding, and make a result reproducible for another developer.

content_blocks.title: The core idea
content_blocks.text: XML is a text-based markup language for structured, hierarchical data. Elements, attributes, character content, and namespaces provide the vocabulary; parsers and applications decide how to use that structure.

content_blocks.title: Connect the subtopics
content_blocks.text: This lesson explicitly covers: Creating a .xml file; Saving XML content; Opening an XML file in a browser or editor; Understanding how different tools display XML. Treat these as connected parts of one workflow: define the structure, make the relevant assumptions explicit, and verify a result with a small known input.

content_blocks.title: Inspectable example: Creating Your First XML File
content_blocks.expected_output: A single well-formed <catalog> root contains a product record, a SKU attribute, and child elements for the product name and price.
content_blocks.run_instructions: Inspect this example as text. Run it only in a processor that supports the shown language/version; the standard CodeLeaf playground previews HTML/CSS/JavaScript only and does not execute XML, XSD, XPath, XSLT, XQuery, Python, or SQL. Start with a tiny document, open it in an XML-aware editor, and verify it is well-formed. XML is not a programming language and does not define application behavior by itself.
content_blocks.reset_steps: Restore the sample to its exact starting state before each experiment. Change one element, attribute, expression, or constraint at a time, then compare the result with the expected behavior.
content_blocks.limitations: This snippet is an inspectable example, not an XML execution service. Validate it with a standards-compatible XML processor; feature support depends on the processor/version.

content_blocks.title: Version and safety checkpoint
content_blocks.text: Distinguish well-formedness, schema validity, and application-level correctness; they are different checks.

content_blocks.title: Try it yourself
content_blocks.text: Create a small synthetic example that demonstrates “Creating a .xml file”. Then add one boundary case involving “Saving XML content”. Write down what should happen before testing, and record the exact output or processor message afterward.

common_mistakes.problem: Assuming a document is correct because it looks readable.
common_mistakes.why: Visual appearance does not prove well-formedness, schema validity, correct namespace handling, or application-level meaning.
common_mistakes.fix: Parse and validate the document with the intended processor, then assert its meaning using a focused test.

common_mistakes.problem: Mixing specification features with processor support.
common_mistakes.why: A standard may define features that a specific runtime does not implement.
common_mistakes.fix: Record the version and feature support; test with the actual target processor.

common_mistakes.why: Missing values, wrong types, namespace differences, or boundary inputs can expose failures.
common_mistakes.fix: Add a valid case, an invalid case, and an edge case to the verification notes.
